children: On August 15, the Prime Minister pledged AI training for one crore young Indians, plus a free online coaching network. Big promises always spark the same question: how do we make them real? What must be built so this becomes a fact, not just a headline?

The urgency is clear. The economy needs skilled youth now, not in 2040. Training one crore in AI is vital, but the bigger prize is using AI to teach nearly 37 crore young Indians everything else they need. Extend it to schools, and learning becomes one seamless journey — from first classroom to first job. No other country has cracked this.

The numbers are sobering. Only 4.2 per cent of working-age Indians have formal vocational training. The India Skills Report 2026 says 44 of every 100 graduates aren’t employable. And the demographic window is closing: the 15-29 age group, nearly 37 crore today, will shrink to 24.5 crore by 2036. Effort and money aren’t missing. What’s missing is design.
India’s education design was built for scarcity. Good teaching was rare, so the system rationed it: standard courses, large batches, narrow gates at fixed ages. Selection stood in for development.
That scarcity is over. India has long known the alternative. In the gurukul, a guru taught many students, yet knew each one: what they grasped, where they struggled, what they could become.

The path and pace were personal. In 1984, researcher Benjamin Bloom showed one-to-one teaching outperforms 98 per cent of classroom learning. AI now makes a guru buildable for every Indian: software that knows what you know, sees where you’re stuck, teaches in your language, adjusts pace and stays until you pass the test a real job demands. When one-to-one teaching stops being scarce, learning no longer needs rationing.

India has done this before. To move money instantly, it built UPI — one shared system any bank or app could connect to. Learning never got such rails, though the building blocks exist: APAAR, the National Credit Framework and Skill India platforms.

Now India must build them. Call it the Kaushal Chakra — a loop that helps every citizen grow. It rests on four pillars: a personal skills passport; a common AI tutoring standard usable by universities, start-ups or ITIs; real teachers paid to mentor in ways software cannot; and an independent body that checks tutoring quality and certifies learning. Together, they create the Kaushal Chakra, a wheel with three stages: Bodh, Abhyas and Siddhi, turning again and again.
Bodh is awareness. The record tracks your learning and shows what you know, what’s close, and where your aptitude points. Suggestions may come, but the decision stays with the person.
Abhyas is development. The guru coaches you through blocks, teaches at your level, and gives practice until the skill is real. Growth no longer waits for admission cycles.

Siddhi is proof. When ready, you attempt the bar a job demands. Whoever taught you never grades you; an independent layer validates the claim and writes it into your passport, trusted by employers anywhere. Then the wheel turns again, building capability across a working life.

Three questions matter. Access: nearly 97 crore Indians are online, and data costs have plunged from ₹269 per gigabyte in 2014 to about 8 today. Teachers: their role grows. Software handles routine teaching, but teachers explain tough concepts, add lessons and step in when a student is about to give up. Employers: they gain a new way to find talent.
Skill becomes a unit — once it’s in your passport, it counts, no matter where you learned it. Apprenticeships, internships, on-the-job training can all be validated.

Start where the Prime Minister pointed. Run the one crore AI-training programme on these rails as the first cohort. Then build capability missions that map emerging jobs and create validated pathways into each. Judge success on two numbers: how much faster people learn, and whether they earn more a year later.
India taught the world that money can move in seconds on public rails. The next proof is waiting: that human capability can move the same way — at each person’s pace, with no ration line in sight.
Sriraj Mallick is the CEO of Infopro Learning. Rahul Patwardhan is a former CEO of NIIT Ltd.

title: One Guru for every Indian
